evidence.claim: Graded dirt roads meet wilderness and an older wagon route in the Sierra.
evidence.quote: Follow this graded dirt road approximately 9 miles

evidence.claim: an older wagon route in the Sierra
evidence.quote: A portion of the Sacatar Trail, an old wagon road into the Owens Valley once used by soldiers and cattlemen, cross the Chimney Peak Wilderness

evidence.claim: The Chimney Peak Backcountry Byway leaves Route 178 at Canebrake for the southern Sierra Nevada.
evidence.quote: The Chimney Peak Back Country Byway splits off from Route 178 in Canebrake, leading to the Chimney Peak Wilderness and connecting to some of the most rugged and remote areas of the Southern Sierra Nevada.

evidence.claim: Canebrake Road is graded dirt; the surrounding wilderness has rocky slopes, pinyon pine and sagebrush.
evidence.quote: Chimney Peak Wilderness encompasses rocky mountainous terrain dominated by pinyon pine with areas of sagebrush.

evidence.claim: The route belongs to the Bureau of Land Management’s backcountry-byway program, which designates secondary roads for automobile tours through or near scenic public lands.
evidence.quote: The BLM began a "byway" program in 1989 which is a tour by automobile through or near scenic public lands. This program designates "backcountry byways" along secondary roads.

evidence.claim: The Bureau of Land Management emphasizes primitive recreation and solitude in this rugged mountain country. Within Chimney Peak Wilderness, springs and streams interrupt the pine and sagebrush terrain, and wildflowers appear seasonally.
evidence.quote: This rugged section of the southern Sierra Nevada mountains offers a number of excellent opportunities for hiking, bakcpacking, day hiking, horseback riding, and outstanding opportunities for primitive recreation and experiences of solitude and isolation.

evidence.claim: Within Chimney Peak Wilderness, springs and streams interrupt the pine and sagebrush terrain, and wildflowers appear seasonally.
evidence.quote: There are scattered springs and streams, with their associated riparian habitat species, and seasonal wildflower displays.

evidence.claim: An older route crosses the wilderness: the Sacatar Trail, a wagon road into the Owens Valley once used by soldiers and cattlemen.
evidence.quote: A portion of the Sacatar Trail, an old wagon road into the Owens Valley once used by soldiers and cattlemen, cross the Chimney Peak Wilderness

evidence.claim: The BLM’s byway program began in 1989, before the wilderness designation.
evidence.quote: The BLM began a "byway" program in 1989

evidence.claim: The California Desert Protection Act created Chimney Peak Wilderness in 1994.
evidence.quote: The 1994 California Desert Protection Act (Public Law 103–433) created the wilderness

evidence.claim: The motor route runs beside part of that protected land.
evidence.quote: A backcountry byway for vehicles is adjacent to part of it.

evidence.claim: Driving north from Route 178, you pass Domelands Wilderness on the left and Owens Peak Wilderness on the right.
evidence.quote: Domelands Wilderness (on your left as you drive up Canebrake Road), Owens Peak Wilderness (on your right as you drive up Canebrake Road)

evidence.claim: Approximately nine miles along Canebrake Road, the Long Valley/Chimney Basin junction divides the approach.
evidence.quote: Follow this graded dirt road approximately 9 miles to the prominent junction of Canebrake and Long Valley/ Chimney Basin Roads.

evidence.claim: The right fork continues toward Chimney Creek Campground; the left leads toward Long Valley Campground.
evidence.quote: continue straight (right fork). The campground will be on the right in an additional 2 miles.

evidence.claim: the left leads toward Long Valley Campground
evidence.quote: Turn left on Long Valley/ Chimney Basin Road and follow it to Long Valley Campgound.

evidence.claim: The byway circles Chimney Peak and returns to Canebrake Road at Lamont Meadow.
evidence.quote: travels through Lamont Meadow, circles around Chimney Peak,  and returns to Canebrake Road at Lamont Meadow.

evidence.claim: Canebrake marks the byway’s departure from Route 178 into the southern Sierra Nevada.
evidence.quote: The Chimney Peak Back Country Byway splits off from Route 178 in Canebrake

evidence.claim: The community lies in the South Fork Valley, beside the creek that the highway follows down from Walker Pass.
evidence.quote: It is located along California State Route 178 in the South Fork Valley

evidence.claim: beside the creek that the highway follows down from Walker Pass
evidence.quote: Canebrake Creek, which State Route 178 follows down to Canebrake from the Walker Pass

evidence.claim: The creek joins the South Fork Kern River at Bloomfield Ranch, part of the Canebrake Ecological Reserve.
evidence.quote: The creek is a major tributary of the South Fork Kern River, which it flows into at Bloomfield Ranch, part of the Canebrake Ecological Reserve.

evidence.claim: The original townsite was about three miles farther east on Isabella-Walker Pass Road.
evidence.quote: The original town site was located about three miles further east on Isabella-Walker Pass Road.

evidence.claim: Robert S. Williamson named Canebrake Creek in the fall of 1853 after a canebrake, or patch of bulrushes. The creek’s name thus describes a plant feature of the place.
evidence.quote: Canebrake Creek, which State Route 178 follows down to Canebrake from the Walker Pass, was named by Robert S. Williamson in the fall of 1853 after he observed Indians there collecting the sugary reeds from a canebrake, or bulrush patch.

evidence.claim: The Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail crosses Canebrake Road just south of Chimney Creek Campground.
evidence.quote: The Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail crosses Canebrake Road just south of the campground.

evidence.claim: The campground occupies an exclusion from Owens Peak Wilderness, with 36 sites beside Chimney Creek at 5,700 feet.
evidence.quote: Chimney Creek Campground is located within Chimney Peak Recreation Area and is cherry stemmed out of Owens Peak Wilderness.

evidence.claim: with 36 sites beside Chimney Creek at 5,700 feet
evidence.quote: The campground contains 36 sites and is nestled among beautiful pinyon pines, grey pines, and oaks along Chimney Creek at 5,700 feet in elevation.

evidence.claim: Pinyon pines, grey pines and oaks grow along the creek.
evidence.quote: pinyon pines, grey pines, and oaks along Chimney Creek at 5,700 feet in elevation.

evidence.claim: A separate primitive path, Chimney Creek Trail, begins at a cattle guard half a mile from the start of the campground road.
evidence.quote: Chimney Creek Trail, a primitive route along Chimney Creek, starts at the cattle guard a half mile from the start of the campground road.

evidence.claim: The campground road branches into spurs serving the sites. The Pacific Crest crossing is on Canebrake Road itself, just south of the campground and its spurs.
evidence.quote: The campground road includes spurs to numerous sites.

evidence.claim: The Pacific Crest crossing is on Canebrake Road itself, just south of the campground and its spurs.
evidence.quote: The Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail crosses Canebrake Road just south of the campground.

evidence.claim: Long Valley Campground occupies an exclusion from Domelands Wilderness.
evidence.quote: Long Valley Campground is a remote, primitive campground located within Chimney Peak Recreation Area and is cherry stemmed out of Domelands Wilderness.

evidence.claim: Its 13 primitive sites lead to a trail connection with the South Fork of the Kern River.
evidence.quote: The campground contains 13 sites, picnic tables, fire rings, and primitive pit toilets.

evidence.claim: The Volpe Trail begins near site 13 at the end of the campground road and runs three miles into the wilderness.
evidence.quote: The Volpe Trail, a 3-mile unmaintained route that provides access to the South Fork of the Kern River within Domelands Wilderness, starts at the end of the campground road near site 13.

evidence.claim: That route is unmaintained.
evidence.quote: a 3-mile unmaintained route

evidence.claim: The two-mile campground access road typically requires a high-clearance 4x4.
evidence.quote: The campground access road is two miles long and typically requires a high clearance 4x4 vehicle.

evidence.claim: A BLM notice dated July 17, 2024 announced Long Valley Campground’s closure for wildland fire danger.
evidence.quote: 7/17/2024- Chimney Peak, Long Valley campgrounds and portion of the Pacific Crest Trail are closed due to wildland fire danger
